RaMP: Runtime-Aware Megakernel Polymorphism for Mixture-of-Experts

Vyom Sharma Affiliation: Hippocratic AI
vyom@hippocraticai.com    Debajyoti Datta Affiliation: Hippocratic AI
debajyoti@hippocraticai.com
Abstract

The optimal kernel configuration for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) inference depends on both batch size and the expert routing distribution—yet every production system dispatches from batch size alone, leaving 10–70% of kernel throughput unrealized. We present RaMP, a routing-aware dispatch framework. A performance-region analysis derives, from hardware constants alone, when each optimization helps—correctly predicting all 8 tested architectures, including 3 unseen. A four-parameter wave cost model selects the fastest configuration from the runtime expert histogram, achieving 0.93%0.93\% mean regret versus exhaustive search, fitted from just 10–24 minutes of one-time profiling per model. Because the model depends only on CTA grid geometry, it is kernel-agnostic: applied to Alpha-MoE, it delivers 1.14×1.14\times with no source modification. Paired with a co-designed CuTe DSL kernel exposing 134–268 polymorphic configurations, RaMP delivers 1.22×1.22\times kernel speedup over static dispatch and 1.30×1.30\times end-to-end speedup in vLLM serving over Triton (1.41×1.41\times over DeepGEMM, 1.13×1.13\times over FlashInfer CUTLASS).

Index Terms: 
mixture-of-experts, kernel dispatch, cost model, GPU optimization, inference serving

I Introduction

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models activate only a fraction of their parameters per token, enabling models with hundreds of billions of parameters at manageable inference cost [1, 2, 3]. The fused MoE kernel—executing up-projection, activation, and down-projection in a single GPU launch—is the critical hot path: on OLMoE-1B-7B, it accounts for over 60% of per-token latency. Modern implementations are already heavily optimized with TMA loads, WGMMA scheduling, and multi-stage pipelines, leaving little room for a single blanket improvement.

The deeper problem is that the optimal kernel configuration depends on the runtime expert routing distribution, which changes at every forward step. Under skewed routing—the norm in production, where only 8–14% of experts are active per layer (§III-A)—a small token block (bm=16\texttt{bm}{=}16) minimizes padding waste. Under balanced routing, a large block (bm=64\texttt{bm}{=}64) reduces wave count. The configuration space is substantial: 134–268 valid tile configurations per model on H200. Yet every production system we examined—vLLM, SGLang, Alpha-MoE, DeepGEMM, FlashInfer—dispatches from batch size alone, ignoring routing entirely. We show that this leaves 10–70% of kernel performance unrealized (§III).

Our key insight is that a physically grounded cost model—encoding startup overhead, wave scheduling, per-CTA memory traffic, and sub-wave nonlinearity as four measurable terms—can dispatch MoE kernels from the actual expert histogram at runtime. Four parameters per configuration, fitted from 25 profiling points in 10–24 minutes, suffice because the model decomposes performance into physically distinct terms. Crucially, the cost model depends only on the CTA grid size, not the kernel implementation: applied to a third-party kernel (Alpha-MoE) with no source modification, it delivers 1.14×1.14\times over their own JIT dispatch (§V-C). The vLLM-specific integration is orthogonal engineering; the cost model framework applies to any fused MoE kernel that exposes a tunable configuration space.

We formalize the conditions under which each kernel optimization helps through four performance-region variables (§IV-A): compute density (ρ\rho), L2 pressure (λ\lambda), wave utilization (ω\omega), and K-reduction depth (κ\kappa). These variables, derived from problem geometry and hardware constants alone, correctly predict optimization applicability for all 8 architectures tested—including 3 unseen models profiled from scratch with no prior knowledge.

Contributions. (1) We characterize the static dispatch problem, showing that routing variation leaves 1.22×1.22\times geomean performance on the table and that three natural alternatives each fail (§III). (2) We introduce a performance-region analysis and four-parameter wave cost model achieving 0.93%0.93\% mean regret versus exhaustive search across 8 architectures, generalizing to unseen models and third-party kernels (§IV-A–IV-B). (3) We co-design a CuTe DSL kernel with 134–268 polymorphic configurations and validate end-to-end in vLLM, delivering 1.30×1.30\times speedup over Triton FP8, 1.41×1.41\times over DeepGEMM, and 1.13×1.13\times over FlashInfer CUTLASS on OLMoE (§IV-C–V-E).

II Background

II-A MoE Inference and Expert Routing

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models partition each feed-forward layer into EE independent expert networks. A lightweight gating network selects the top-kk experts per token, routing each token to only a small fraction of the total parameters. This conditional computation enables models with hundreds of billions of parameters while activating only a few billion per token: OLMoE [2] contains 7B total parameters but activates only 1B, and DeepSeek-V3 [1] contains 671B with 37B active.

Crucially, the routing decision is input-dependent: different tokens activate different expert subsets, and the distribution changes at every forward step. We quantify routing skew via entropy-normalized balancedness β=H⁡(𝐜)/ln⁡E\beta=H(\mathbf{c})/\ln E (β=1\beta{=}1: uniform; lower values: skewed). The trend toward fine-grained MoE (DeepSeek-V3: E=256E{=}256; Qwen3: E=128E{=}128) amplifies this variability, making the optimal kernel configuration increasingly input-dependent (§III-A).

II-B Fused MoE Kernel Anatomy

A fused MoE kernel executes all three phases of the expert computation in a single GPU launch: Phase 1 (up-projection) loads expert weight tiles via TMA and computes 𝐇e=𝐗e​𝐖1,e\mathbf{H}_{e}=\mathbf{X}_{e}\mathbf{W}_{1,e} through WGMMA matrix-multiply-accumulate instructions; Phase 2 applies the SwiGLU nonlinearity with in-register FP8 re-quantization, avoiding any write to HBM; Phase 3 (down-projection) computes the final output and scatters it back to the token positions via atomic add. By keeping the intermediate activations in registers between phases, the fused kernel eliminates two HBM round-trips per expert per token that a multi-kernel implementation would incur.

On Hopper GPUs, each CTA uses warp specialization: 128 producer threads issue TMA weight loads and cp.async activation gathers into a multi-stage shared memory pipeline, while wn×32\texttt{wn}\times 32 consumer threads drain the pipeline through WGMMA instructions that read directly from shared memory descriptors. The producer fills the next pipeline stage while the consumer computes on the current one, overlapping memory latency with compute.

The kernel is parameterized by a tile configuration c=(bm,bn,wn,stg)c=(\texttt{bm},\texttt{bn},\texttt{wn},\texttt{stg}), specifying the token block size (how many tokens each CTA processes), weight sub-tile width, consumer warp count, and pipeline depth (number of buffered stages), respectively. The CTA grid depends on the expert token distribution:

grid⁡(c)=∑e⌈ce/bm⌉⏟M-tiles (routing-dependent)×⌈N/(bn⋅wn)⌉⏟N-tiles (config-dependent)\mathrm{grid}(c)=\underbrace{\textstyle\sum_{e}\lceil c_{e}/\texttt{bm}\rceil}_{\text{M-tiles (routing-dependent)}}\times\underbrace{\lceil N/(\texttt{bn}\cdot\texttt{wn})\rceil}_{\text{N-tiles (config-dependent)}} (1)

Because the M-tiles term depends on the routing distribution, different values of β\beta at the same batch size SS produce grids differing by 1.6−10×1.6{-}10\times (Figure 1), which in turn demand different configurations.

II-C Existing Dispatch Approaches

Table I summarizes the dispatch strategy of production MoE systems. All share a fundamental limitation: they select configurations from batch size alone, ignoring the routing distribution. Moreover, adding a new optimization dimension (e.g., GROUP_M swizzle) doubles the search space, causing autotuning costs to scale combinatorially. The next section quantifies the performance cost of this static approach.

III Challenges and Opportunities

Before presenting our solution, we characterize the static dispatch problem quantitatively: how much performance do production systems leave on the table by ignoring the routing distribution?

III-A Routing Variation in Production

We instrument OLMoE (E=64E{=}64) and Qwen3 (E=128E{=}128) with routing hooks on four downstream tasks (MMLU, GSM8K, code generation, and open-ended chat; 12 prompts per model, yielding 9,728 and 192,103 per-layer routing observations, respectively).

Real MoE routing is deeply skewed (Figure 2): only 8−14%8{-}14\% of experts are active per layer on both models, and β\beta falls below 0.70.7 over 96%96\% of the time. The distribution is tightly concentrated: on OLMoE, 96.9% of 9,728 per-layer observations fall within β∈[0.50,0.60)\beta\in[0.50,0.60) (std= 0.06\,{=}\,0.06). This has two implications: (1) static dispatch tuned at β=1.0\beta{=}1.0 is systematically mismatched with the β≈0.5\beta\approx 0.5 regime that dominates production, and (2) a cost model evaluated near β=0.5\beta{=}0.5 generalizes to nearly all real traffic.

Takeaway 1: Real MoE routing is deeply skewed (β≈0.5\beta\approx 0.5, only 8–14% of experts active), yet every production system dispatches as though routing were uniform (β=1.0\beta{=}1.0).

Why skew hurts: wave utilization.  Figure 3 reveals the mechanism. For a fixed tile size bm, skewed routing produces uneven CTA counts across experts, fragmenting the grid into partially filled waves. At typical operating points (β≈0.5\beta\approx 0.5), small batches lose 15–30% of SM occupancy compared to the uniform assumption, and even large batches see measurable degradation—explaining why a single bm tuned at β=1.0\beta{=}1.0 under-performs in production.

III-B Performance Left on the Table

To quantify the resulting gap, we profile OLMoE with vLLM’s default Triton FP8 config at 24 operating points (6 batch sizes ×\times 4 balancedness levels) and compare against the best available config from our 134-config pool, using 50-iteration median timing per config per point.

At 22 of the 24 operating points, a different configuration outperforms vLLM’s default, by up to 70%70\% at decode (S=32S{=}32, β=0.5\beta{=}0.5) and by 10−25%10{-}25\% at moderate batch sizes. The aggregate opportunity amounts to a 1.22×1.22\times geomean speedup if the correct config could be selected at every point.

Figure 4 visualizes the full operating space: OLMoE requires 6 unique configs and DSv3-TP8 requires 8 to cover all (S,β)(S,\beta) points—no single configuration dominates.

III-C Why Simpler Approaches Fall Short

Three natural responses to this problem each prove insufficient:

Approach 1: Finer-grained bucket dispatch. Triton’s lookup rounds MM to the nearest power-of-2 anchor. Doubling the number of anchors captures batch-size variation more precisely, achieving 1.05×1.05\times geomean improvement over standard buckets. However, this approach still misses routing variation within a bucket: two invocations with the same MM but different β\beta require different configs.

Approach 2: Exhaustive online search. Evaluating all 134 configs at each invocation would cost 134×48​μ​s=6.4​ms134\times 48\,\mu\text{s}=6.4\,\text{ms}, which is orders of magnitude larger than the 20−300​μ20{-}300\,\mus kernel it aims to optimize. Runtime exhaustive search is impractical.

Approach 3: Simple linear cost model. A 2-parameter model (T=a+b×gridT=a+b\times\mathrm{grid}) captures the gross scaling trend but misses wave quantization: kernel time jumps sharply at CTA grid multiples of SM​_​COUNT=132\mathrm{SM\_COUNT}{=}132. On DSv3 (N=512N{=}512, yielding only 2 N-tiles), this model produces 37.5%37.5\% max regret because the grid-time relationship is concave in the sub-wave region rather than linear.

Takeaway 2: An effective dispatch must be (a) sub-50​μ50\,\mus for runtime use, (b) routing-aware (dispatching from the expert histogram, not MM alone), and (c) physically grounded to capture wave quantization.

IV RaMP: System Design

RaMP addresses the three shortcomings identified in §III through three components (Figure 5): a performance-region analysis that identifies when each optimization helps (§IV-A), a wave cost model that predicts which config is fastest at runtime (§IV-B), and a co-designed kernel that provides the configuration diversity the cost model requires (§IV-C).

IV-A MoE Performance Regions

On a highly-optimized fused MoE kernel, no single optimization helps universally. GROUP_M swizzle is essential on Mixtral but irrelevant on OLMoE. Split-K fills idle SMs on DSv3 at decode batch sizes but degrades performance on Mixtral. Small token blocks reduce padding under skewed routing but increase wave count under balanced routing. The question, therefore, is not how to make the kernel faster in general, but rather when each optimization helps and how to select the right combination at runtime.

We answer this question by identifying four variables from the problem geometry (E,N,K)(E,N,K), each targeting a specific hardware bottleneck. For each variable, we explain why it captures an effect that no simpler metric addresses.

Compute density (ρ\rho):

ρ=N⋅Kttn⋅tile_k\rho=\frac{N\cdot K}{\texttt{ttn}\cdot\texttt{tile\_k}} (2)

This quantity counts the number of WGMMA tile operations per CTA. Why not use raw FLOPs or arithmetic intensity instead? Raw FLOPs ignore pipeline overhead, which dominates at small grids: each CTA pays a fixed startup cost (pipeline fill, mbarrier setup, TMA descriptor initialization) regardless of compute volume. Arithmetic intensity (FLOPs/byte) captures the balance between compute and memory bandwidth, but not between compute and pipeline fill. By contrast, ρ\rho captures precisely this ratio. When ρ<ρc\rho<\rho_{c}, startup overhead exceeds useful compute per CTA, and the kernel becomes pipeline-dominated. The critical threshold ρc≈186\rho_{c}\approx 186 follows from the ratio of single-CTA startup cost (24​μ24\,\mus median on H200) to effective WGMMA throughput (130130 ns/tile including pipeline stalls), consistent with the empirically observed crossover at ρc≈200\rho_{c}\approx 200.

L2 pressure (λ\lambda, κ\kappa):

λ=⌈N/ttn⌉,κ=K/tile_k\lambda=\lceil N/\texttt{ttn}\rceil,\qquad\kappa=K/\texttt{tile\_k} (3)

In a fused MoE kernel, the dominant memory pattern is weight loading via TMA. When two CTAs processing different M-tiles for the same expert execute concurrently, they access the same weight column; if it remains in L2, the second CTA avoids an HBM fetch. L2 is the only level where inter-CTA weight reuse occurs: L1 is per-SM and holds only the current pipeline stage, while registers and shared memory hold accumulators and buffers, not prior tiles.

GROUP_M swizzle addresses L2 pressure by reordering the CTA grid so that groups of adjacent M-tiles share weight columns before advancing. The condition is whether the weight footprint exceeds effective L2 capacity. With L​2eff=0.75×60​MB=45L2_{\mathrm{eff}}=0.75\times 60\,\mathrm{MB}=45 MB (NCU confirms 72–78% of L2 sectors available for weights):

λ⋅κ>L​2effttn⋅tile_k⋅sizeof⁡(FP8)=45​MB32​KB=1440\lambda\cdot\kappa>\frac{L2_{\mathrm{eff}}}{\texttt{ttn}\cdot\texttt{tile\_k}\cdot\mathrm{sizeof(FP8)}}=\frac{45\,\mathrm{MB}}{32\,\mathrm{KB}}=1440 (4)

This threshold correctly predicts GROUP_M applicability for all 8 models with zero exceptions (Table III): Mixtral (λ⋅κ=6144\lambda\cdot\kappa=6144) and the three Regime-B unseen models exceed it, while OLMoE (128128) and DSv3 (112112) fall far below.

Wave utilization (ω\omega):

ω=grid⁡(c,S,routing)/SM​_​COUNT\omega=\mathrm{grid}(c,S,\text{routing})\;/\;\mathrm{SM\_COUNT} (5)

Why measure waves rather than SM occupancy? SM occupancy (warps per SM) is a per-SM metric that quantifies instruction-level parallelism within a single SM. The variable ω\omega captures a qualitatively different phenomenon: GPU-wide grid quantization. Increasing the grid from 131 CTAs (ω=0.99\omega{=}0.99, one nearly-full wave) to 133 CTAs (ω=1.01\omega{=}1.01, two waves with the second nearly empty) approximately doubles wall-clock time. This quantization cliff is invisible to occupancy metrics. Notably, ω\omega is the only routing-dependent variable: different expert distributions at the same batch size SS produce different ω\omega values, which in turn select different configurations.

K-reduction depth (κ\kappa): κ=K/tile_k\kappa=K/\texttt{tile\_k}. Why treat this separately from ρ\rho? A deep K-dimension creates a qualitatively different opportunity: splitting the K-reduction across multiple CTAs (split-K) can fill idle SMs at sub-wave operating points. This technique is beneficial only when κ≥48\kappa\geq 48 and ω<0.2\omega<0.2. Split-K with sk=4\mathrm{sk}{=}4 quadruples the grid, so the original grid must contain fewer than 33 CTAs for the expanded grid to remain within one wave. At higher ω\omega, the two-launch overhead (approximately 10−15​μ10{-}15\,\mus) outweighs the parallelism benefit, causing split-K to degrade performance. The threshold κ≥48\kappa\geq 48 ensures that sufficient reduction work exists to amortize this overhead. The distinction from ρ\rho is fundamental: ρ\rho measures compute density per CTA, while κ\kappa measures reduction depth across CTAs (Figure 6).

These four variables are sufficient because they cover the hardware axes that vary across operating points: per-CTA compute (ρ\rho), cache pressure (λ\lambda), grid-level parallelism (ω\omega), and reduction depth (κ\kappa). Register pressure, shared memory limits, and TMA alignment constrain which configs exist but do not vary at runtime.

Region classification. These variables partition the operating space into distinct regions (Table II).

Model classification. Table III classifies eight production MoE architectures, and Figure 7 visualizes them in the (λ,ρ)(\lambda,\rho) plane. The first five were used during development; the last three (italicized) are completely unseen models, profiled from scratch during evaluation with no prior knowledge. “Unseen” means no model-specific development or tuning was performed; the same profiling recipe (enumerate configs, time at 25 points, OLS fit) applies to any new architecture in 10–24 minutes. The cost model form generalizes across architectures; per-target profiling calibrates its parameters.

IV-B Wave-Based Cost Model

The performance regions identify which optimizations are applicable to a given model. We now construct the cost model that selects which specific configuration is fastest for the actual routing distribution observed at runtime.

Formulation. We decompose a fused MoE kernel’s execution time into four terms, each capturing a physically distinct component of GPU kernel scheduling:

T⁡(c)=a⁡(c)⏟startup+b⁡(c)​gSM⏟waves+c⁡(c)​g⏟per-CTA+d⁡(c)​log⁡(g+1)⏟sub-waveT(c)=\underbrace{a(c)}_{\text{startup}}+\underbrace{b(c)\,\tfrac{g}{\mathrm{SM}}}_{\text{waves}}+\underbrace{c(c)\,g\vphantom{\tfrac{g}{S}}}_{\text{per-CTA}}+\underbrace{d(c)\,\log(g{+}1)\vphantom{\tfrac{g}{S}}}_{\text{sub-wave}} (6)

where g=grid⁡(c,routing)g=\mathrm{grid}(c,\text{routing}) is the CTA count from Eq. 1 and SM=132\mathrm{SM}{=}132 on H200.

Term-by-term interpretation. (1) a⁡(c)a(c): the startup cost of one CTA—pipeline fill, mbarrier initialization, TMA descriptor setup—independent of how many CTAs run. (2) b⁡(c)×g/SMb(c)\times g/\mathrm{SM}: the cost of wave scheduling; g/SMg/\mathrm{SM} counts how many sequential waves the GPU must execute. The continuous ratio g/SMg/\mathrm{SM} (rather than ⌈g/SM⌉\lceil g/\mathrm{SM}\rceil) linearizes the wave count; the staircase jumps at wave boundaries are absorbed into the c×gc\times g term during OLS fitting. (3) c⁡(c)×gc(c)\times g: the cost that scales per CTA, dominated by HBM weight traffic. Each CTA loads one weight tile (ttn×tile_k\texttt{ttn}\times\texttt{tile\_k} bytes); more CTAs means more total traffic when L2 misses. (4) d⁡(c)×log⁡(g+1)d(c)\times\log(g{+}1): captures diminishing returns of CTA parallelism in the sub-wave regime (g<SMg<\mathrm{SM}), where adding CTAs to a partially-filled wave provides decreasing marginal utilization.

Because gg depends on the routing distribution (Eq. 1), TT becomes a function of both the configuration and the runtime expert histogram.

Why not merge the wave and CTA terms? The coefficients b/SMb/\mathrm{SM} and cc are fitted independently by OLS and capture different physical effects: bb tracks SM scheduling overhead (constant per wave), while cc tracks memory traffic (proportional to the number of CTAs). Models with high λ\lambda (many N-tiles, high L2 pressure) exhibit large cc but small bb; models with low λ\lambda show the reverse. Merging them into a single k×gk\times g term forces a shared coefficient, increasing mean regret from 0.93%0.93\% to 8.1%8.1\%.

Progressive refinement. We validate each term’s contribution through ablation (§V-B). The 3-param model separates wave and CTA effects, halving mean regret. The 4th term (log\log) is critical for DSv3’s sub-wave regime (ntiles=2n_{\mathrm{tiles}}{=}2, grid always <SM<\mathrm{SM}), where the grid-time curve is concave rather than linear; it reduces DSv3’s max regret from 37.5%37.5\% to 1.5%1.5\%. A 5th term (g2g^{2}) provides negligible further improvement, confirming four terms are sufficient.

The log⁡(g+1)\log(g{+}1) term activates adaptively: it is included only for configs whose median profiling grid falls below SM​_​COUNT\mathrm{SM\_COUNT} (the sub-wave region). Configs with larger grids use the 3-parameter base (d=0d{=}0). This selective activation prevents overfitting on multi-wave models while capturing sub-wave concavity on architectures like DSv3.

Fitting. Three or four parameters per config are fitted via ordinary least squares from profiling at 5 batch sizes ×\times 5 balancedness levels =25=25 points per config. Why OLS rather than a learned model? We compared OLS against a Random Forest (50 trees, max depth 5) and an MLP (32×\times16 hidden units) trained on the same 25 points per config with features [g/SM,g,log⁡(g+1)][g/\mathrm{SM},g,\log(g{+}1)]. On held-out test points, the MLP achieves 2.0%2.0\% mean regret (vs. OLS 6.8%6.8\%), but with 624 parameters per config fitted from 25 samples, it is severely overparameterized. OLS wins on deployment cost (4 floats per config, no ML framework dependency), physical interpretability (a≈a\approx pipeline fill, b≈b\approx wave overhead, c≈c\approx per-CTA traffic), and cross-architecture generalization—the parameters cluster by performance region (§V-D) because they capture hardware physics, not model-specific artifacts. Fitting requires a single matrix solve (under 1 ms per config). End-to-end profiling takes 10–24 minutes per model.

Extensibility. Adding a new optimization dimension (e.g., GROUP_M) appends CnewC_{\mathrm{new}} configs to the pool and profiles them at the same 25 points. The profiling cost grows linearly in the number of dimensions, not multiplicatively as in combinatorial autotuning.

Runtime dispatch. At serving time, the cost model evaluates all configs against the current expert histogram via a single fused Triton kernel on GPU that performs a bincount, vectorized cost evaluation, and argmin, all in approximately 38​μ38\,\mus. The dispatch result is cached per step and keyed on total token count MM; subsequent MoE layers reuse the cached config. At each new step, the cache is cleared and the first layer re-dispatches from the fresh routing histogram. The total memory footprint is 4 floats ×\times 268 configs ×\times 4 bytes =4.3=4.3 KB per model.

IV-C Co-Designed Fused MoE Kernel

A routing-aware cost model requires a configuration space wide enough to exploit routing variation. Alpha-MoE exposes 2 tile families; DeepGEMM fixes bm=128\texttt{bm}{=}128. We implement a 1,738-line CuTe DSL [9] fused 3-phase kernel (W8A8 FP8, 128×128128{\times}128 block scales) that exposes 134–268 valid configurations per model on H200.

The kernel implements the standard fused MoE forward pass: Phase 1 gathers token activations via cp.async and computes up-projection through WGMMA; Phase 2 applies SwiGLU with in-register FP8 re-quantization (no HBM write); Phase 3 computes down-projection and scatters via cp.reduce.async.bulk. Producer-consumer warp specialization with stg-deep pipelines hides TMA latency.

Configuration diversity. Hardware constraints (shared memory ≤227\leq 227 KB, register budgets, WGMMA alignment) yield 134 valid configs for Regime-A models and 268 for Regime-B (GROUP_M variants included). Configs span four tile families (ttn∈{256,512}\texttt{ttn}\in\{256,512\}), pipeline depths 1–5, and token blocks bm∈[2,104]\texttt{bm}\in[2,104]. Two design choices expand the space: dynamic register allocation (supporting bm up to 104 vs. 72 in prior work) and grid overlaunch (upper-bound grid with early-exit, eliminating GPU-to-CPU sync for exact grid computation).

Polymorphic modes. GROUP_M swizzle, split-K (sk=4\mathrm{sk}{=}4 in grid z-dimension), tile families, and compile variants are all selected at compile time but dispatched at runtime by the cost model. Split-K partitions Phase 1’s K-reduction across 4 CTAs, filling idle SMs at sub-wave operating points (Figure 6). CuTe DSL compiles each configuration in ∼5{\sim}5 s via TVM-FFI JIT.

IV-D Runtime Dispatch

At serving time (Figure 5), a single fused Triton kernel performs three operations: (1) expert histogram via atomic bincount, (2) vectorized cost evaluation of Eq. 6 for all configs, and (3) argmin to select the optimal config. Total latency: ∼38​μ{\sim}38\,\mus, amortized to <2.5​μ{<}2.5\,\mus per MoE layer via per-step caching. The result is transferred to Python via a single .item() call; no additional CPU-GPU sync occurs.

Both static and routing-aware modes launch the same compiled kernel binary—the only difference is config selection. Any observed speedup is therefore attributable to better dispatch, not kernel implementation differences.

The cost model formulation (Eq. 6) depends only on the CTA grid, not the kernel. Profiling a new backend requires only timing its configs at 25 (S,β)(S,\beta) points and fitting via OLS; no source modification is needed. This kernel-agnostic property is validated experimentally in Table VI.

Per-step amortization. The dispatch result is cached for all MoE layers within a single forward step. This is justified by the low cross-layer β\beta variance (0.00080.0008, measured across 9,728 per-layer observations); per-layer dispatch provides only 1.02−1.04×1.02{-}1.04\times additional gain (§V-E). The total memory footprint is 4 floats ×\times 268 configs ×\times 4 bytes =4.3=4.3 KB per model.

V Evaluation

We evaluate RaMP at two levels. Kernel-level evaluation (§V-B–V-D) constitutes the primary research evaluation: it validates the cost model’s accuracy, the routing-aware dispatch thesis, the kernel-agnostic property, and the regime theory’s predictions under controlled conditions. End-to-end serving (§V-E) validates that kernel-level gains translate to measurable improvements in a production serving stack.

V-A Methodology

Hardware. Single NVIDIA H200 SXM (132 SMs, 4.8 TB/s HBM3e, SM 90a); CUDA 12.8, PyTorch 2.9, CUTLASS 4.0.

Protocol. Kernel: CUDA events, 10 warmup + 50 timed iterations, median reported (CV<3%{<}3\% for 99% of points). E2E: vLLM v0.9, --enforce-eager, 80 prompts, sequential same-GPU runs with full server restart between backends.

Baselines. Exhaustive search: all 134–268 configs timed at every point (ceiling). Static dispatch: best config at β=1.0\beta{=}1.0. Alpha-MoE [5]: JIT-tuned C++ kernel. vLLM Triton FP8: production default. FlashInfer CUTLASS [7]: integrated CUTLASS/TRT-LLM kernels.

V-B Cost Model Accuracy

Table IV reports cost model regret against exhaustive search across 8 architectures (5 known, 3 unseen). The model achieves 0.93%\mathbf{0.93\%} mean regret overall and 0.91%\mathbf{0.91\%} on unseen models—lower than the known-model average, confirming that no model-specific tuning is needed. Test points include S=1024S{=}1024 (exceeding the profiling maximum of 512) and β∈{0.2,0.8}\beta\in\{0.2,0.8\} (absent from profiling), demonstrating extrapolation.

The max regret (10.2%10.2\% on Qwen3 at S=8S{=}8, β=0.8\beta{=}0.8) occurs at an edge case where each expert receives ≤1\leq 1 token, making the CTA grid identical for every bm; the absolute gap is only 6.5​μ6.5\,\mus. In practice, β>0.7\beta>0.7 occurs in only 2.5%2.5\% of observations.

Progressive refinement. The ablation from 2 to 4 parameters validates each term’s necessity:

Model Mean regret Max regret
2-param: a+k⋅ga+k\cdot g 8.1% 42.3%
3-param: a+b⋅g/SM+c⋅ga+b\cdot g/\mathrm{SM}+c\cdot g 4.0% 37.5%
4-param: +d⋅log(g+1)+\;d\cdot\log(g{+}1) 0.93% 10.2%

The log⁡(g+1)\log(g{+}1) term alone reduces DSv3’s max regret from 37.5%37.5\% to 1.5%1.5\%. The cost model achieves R2≥0.88R^{2}\geq 0.88 on all 8 models, with profiling taking 10–24 minutes per model.

V-C Kernel-Level Evaluation

This section presents the primary research evaluation: kernel throughput under controlled routing conditions.

How much does routing-aware dispatch help? Table V evaluates the central question: does adapting to the routing distribution yield improvement over strong static policies? Static dispatch is defined as the best config at β=1.0\beta{=}1.0—the policy all existing autotuners produce.

At realistic routing (β=0.5\beta{=}0.5), routing-aware dispatch provides 1.22×\mathbf{1.22\times} geomean speedup, reaching 1.70×1.70\times on DSv3-TP8 at S=64S{=}64. Even at β=0.8\beta{=}0.8 (moderate skew), gains persist at 1.03−1.08×1.03{-}1.08\times. This result isolates the value of routing information: same kernel, same hardware, only the dispatch strategy differs.

Is the cost model kernel-agnostic? To demonstrate that the cost model is not tied to our kernel, we profile Alpha-MoE’s C++ kernel through our cost model and compare against their JIT dispatch—same kernel binary, different config selection (Table VI).

The dispatch column isolates the cost model’s contribution on an unmodified third-party kernel: our routing-aware dispatch improves Alpha-MoE’s own kernel by 1.14×\mathbf{1.14\times} geomean, with only 1 loss out of 92 test points. This confirms that the cost model framework applies to any fused MoE kernel exposing a tunable config space; the vLLM-specific integration details are orthogonal. Profiling a new kernel requires only 10–24 min of timing; no source modification is needed.

Combined kernel + dispatch (Table VII). The full RaMP system (CuTe kernel + cost model) achieves 1.21×\mathbf{1.21\times} geomean over Alpha-MoE across 4 models, with the largest gain on Mixtral (1.45×1.45\times) where GROUP_M reduces L2 thrashing.

V-D Performance-Region Validation

The regime theory makes falsifiable predictions from hardware constants alone. We validate each via Nsight Compute profiling and standalone kernel experiments.

NCU validation (Table VIII). ρ\rho predicts TC utilization (below 20% for all models, confirming pipeline domination); λ\lambda predicts L2 hit rate (models with λ>8\lambda>8 show persistent thrashing); ω\omega predicts SM occupancy (DSv3-EP8 at 18.8% through S=64S{=}64, confirming split-K opportunity).

Split-K: predicted before implemented. The regime analysis predicted split-K on DSv3 (κ=56\kappa{=}56, ω<0.2\omega<0.2) from geometry alone, before any split-K kernel existed. The subsequently implemented kernel confirms: 1.11−1.12×1.11{-}1.12\times on DSv3 (positive prediction) and 0.83−0.88×0.83{-}0.88\times on Mixtral/DBRX (negative prediction). Both positive and negative confirmations carry equal evidential weight.

GROUP_M: threshold-exact. Eq. 4 correctly predicts GROUP_M necessity for all 8 models: required on Mixtral (λ⋅κ=6144≫1440\lambda\cdot\kappa=6144\gg 1440, 1.15−1.29×1.15{-}1.29\times at S≥128S\geq 128), irrelevant on OLMoE (λ⋅κ=128≪1440\lambda\cdot\kappa=128\ll 1440).

V-E End-to-End System Validation

To validate that kernel-level gains translate to real serving improvements, we deploy RaMP in vLLM and benchmark against all available backends.

Table IX reports RaMP speedup across two workload profiles—long-context (1024-token input, 32-token output) and ShareGPT (real conversation traces)—at request rates r=2−8r{=}2{-}8. Across all 5 configurations, RaMP achieves 1.30×\mathbf{1.30\times} TPOT geomean over Triton FP8, 1.41×\mathbf{1.41\times} over DeepGEMM, and 1.13×\mathbf{1.13\times} over FlashInfer CUTLASS, with 1.17×\mathbf{1.17\times} TTFT improvement over Triton. DeepGEMM’s fixed bm=128\texttt{bm}{=}128 is poorly matched to OLMoE’s small expert sizes (1.24−1.50×1.24{-}1.50\times). RaMP outperforms FlashInfer on every configuration (1.09−1.16×1.09{-}1.16\times TPOT), confirming that routing-aware dispatch provides gains beyond what CUTLASS autotuning achieves alone.

E2E attribution. The TPOT improvement decomposes into ∼1.05×{\sim}1.05\times from the fused CuTe kernel (eliminating inter-phase HBM traffic) and ∼1.12×{\sim}1.12\times from routing-aware dispatch. The dispatch contribution—the paper’s primary claim—accounts for the majority of the E2E gain.

Second model: Qwen3.5-A3B (E=256E{=}256, top-k=8k{=}8, 40 MoE layers). Profiled from scratch in 12 minutes with no model-specific tuning, this model achieves 1.10×\mathbf{1.10\times} geomean TPOT improvement (1.08−1.11×1.08{-}1.11\times across 6 workload configurations), confirming generalization to unseen architectures in deployment.

VI Related Work

MoE training systems. MegaBlocks [10], Tutel [11], FasterMoE [12], and ScatterMoE [13] optimize communication and compute for MoE training. SonicMoE [8] achieves near-roofline training throughput via IO-overlapping kernels. These address training; our work targets single-GPU inference dispatch.

MoE inference kernels. Alpha-MoE [5] provides a JIT-tuned fused kernel (∼2{\sim}2 hours per model); DeepGEMM [6] offers JIT-compiled grouped GEMM with fixed bm=128\texttt{bm}{=}128; FlashInfer [7] integrates CUTLASS kernels with autotuning. All use static per-MM dispatch. Our cost model is kernel-agnostic: it improved Alpha-MoE’s own kernel by 1.14×1.14\times (§V-C) without source modification.

Autotuning and performance modeling. vLLM [4], SGLang [14], and Triton [15] select configs via offline sweeps; TVM/Ansor [16] searches via learned cost models. All scale combinatorially with optimization dimensions and produce static dispatch tables; our wave model adds new dimensions at linear profiling cost. The roofline model [17] classifies compute- vs. memory-bound kernels; the ECM model [18] adds cache hierarchy effects. Our region analysis extends this to MoE dispatch: where roofline predicts bottleneck type, our variables predict which specific optimizations help, with thresholds derived from hardware constants.

VII Conclusion

We presented RaMP, demonstrating that routing-aware kernel dispatch is a fundamental missing axis in MoE inference optimization. A performance-region analysis derived from hardware constants identifies when each optimization helps across all 8 tested architectures. A four-parameter wave cost model achieves 0.93%0.93\% mean regret and 1.22×1.22\times kernel speedup over static dispatch. Because the model depends only on CTA grid geometry, it is kernel-agnostic: applied to Alpha-MoE with no source changes, it delivers 1.14×1.14\times. Deployed in vLLM, the full system achieves 1.30×1.30\times end-to-end speedup over Triton FP8, 1.41×1.41\times over DeepGEMM, and 1.13×1.13\times over FlashInfer CUTLASS on OLMoE, and 1.10×1.10\times on Qwen3.5-A3B.

Limitations. (1) Validated on Hopper W8A8 FP8; extending to Blackwell requires re-profiling but not re-derivation. (2) Single-GPU scope; expert-parallel communication is orthogonal. (3) At S=1S{=}1 or under perfectly uniform routing (β=1\beta{=}1), routing-aware and static dispatch converge by design. As MoE architectures continue to scale expert counts and routing complexity, we believe routing-aware dispatch will become a standard component of inference serving stacks.
